lesson.title: The Cell's Protein Factory: Inside the Ribosome
lesson.summary: A ribosome is a two-part molecular machine, built from ribosomal RNA and protein, that reads mRNA and assembles amino acids into a growing protein chain.
lesson.body:
Every protein a cell makes is built by a ribosome, and every ribosome is built from two pieces: a large subunit and a small subunit, each one a complex of ribosomal RNA and protein together, not protein alone. In the cytoplasm of a eukaryotic cell, the small subunit is referred to as the 40S subunit and the large subunit as the 60S subunit; when they come together on an mRNA to begin translation, they form the complete 80S ribosome. The S values describe how quickly each particle settles during centrifugation and depend on shape as well as mass, which is why the numbers for the two subunits do not simply add up to the number for the whole ribosome.

The two subunits are not built from scratch out in the cytoplasm. They are assembled in the nucleolus, the structure inside the nucleus dedicated to exactly this job. There, ribosomal RNA is transcribed and processed, then combined with ribosomal proteins that were made in the cytoplasm and imported back into the nucleus for assembly. Once each subunit is complete, it is exported separately through a nuclear pore into the cytoplasm, and the two subunits remain apart until they meet up on an mRNA molecule to start translating.

Where a ribosome ends up working depends on what kind of protein it is making, a distinction that only exists because eukaryotic cells are internally compartmentalized. Free ribosomes, floating in the cytosol, typically make proteins that will stay in the cytoplasm or be sent to organelles like mitochondria or the nucleus. Bound ribosomes, docked onto the rough endoplasmic reticulum, make proteins destined for secretion, insertion into membranes, or delivery to organelles such as lysosomes. The ribosome itself is structurally identical in both locations; what differs is simply where translation is happening and where the finished protein is headed. Inside every one of these ribosomes, regardless of location, there are three specific binding sites for tRNA that will matter enormously once we look at how translation actually proceeds step by step.
